facts.claim: Nicholle Acciarri was scheduled to fly from New York to Cleveland when she was denied boarding; she claimed a gate agent offered a $650 check or reimbursement for a rental car, airline ticket or hotel, and she rented a car and drove to Cleveland expecting American to cover the expense.

The airline initially provided a $250 flight credit that expired after one year; customer relations later said she was not entitled to regulated compensation because the aircraft had been changed to a smaller model, and one supervisor reportedly found records indicating eligibility for a $353 check or a $442 credit due to weight restrictions, which American subsequently described as an error.

After consumer advocate Christopher Elliott contacted the airline, American issued an additional $192 credit, bringing the total to $442; the carrier acknowledged an agent had made an offer at the airport but declined to pay $650, suggesting that amount was likely intended for passengers volunteering to give up their seats, and Elliott's report does not establish whether the gate agent had authority to guarantee the larger payment.

Under 14 CFR 250.6, passengers are not eligible for involuntary denied-boarding compensation when a lower-capacity aircraft is substituted for operational or safety reasons and the change prevents the flight from accommodating everyone with confirmed reservations.

For eligible involuntary bumps, Department of Transportation limits reach 200% of the one-way fare, capped at $1,075, for qualifying delays, and 400%, capped at $2,150, for longer delays; those amounts do not apply automatically when the smaller-aircraft exception is triggered.

American directed airport employees to stop involuntarily denying boarding, effective September 30, 2026; staff were instructed to keep aircraft doors open until enough passengers volunteered to change flights, even if departure had to be delayed, and airport managers can approve higher offers.

Department of Transportation figures cited by View From The Wing show American and its regional partners bumped 14,758 passengers in 2025, about 60% of the 24,596 involuntary denied boardings reported across the industry; American recorded more such cases than all other reporting airlines combined, although Frontier had the highest rate relative to passenger volume.
The DOT requires airlines to provide involuntarily bumped passengers with a written explanation of their rights.

zh.title: 美航拒付承諾的650美元補償，稱換小飛機不適用非自願拒載賠償
zh.summary: 美國航空拒絕兌現地勤人員據稱向一名被拒登機旅客承諾的650美元，理由是航班換成較小機型，依聯邦規定不適用非自願拒載賠償；旅客最終僅獲得總計442美元的飛行抵用金。此案發生在美航9月30日起要求停止非自願拒載的數週後。
body: 尼科爾·阿恰里（Nicholle Acciarri）原定自紐約搭機前往克里夫蘭，卻被拒絕登機。她表示，地勤人員曾承諾提供650美元支票，或補償租車、機票或飯店費用；她隨後租車開往克里夫蘭，期待美航負擔費用。美航最初僅提供250美元飛行抵用金、一年後到期；客服其後表示，由於航班改用較小機型，她不符合法定賠償資格。一名主管據稱曾查到紀錄顯示她可獲得353美元支票或442美元抵用金，原因是重量限制，但美航其後稱該筆紀錄有誤。
消費者權益倡議者克里斯多福·艾略特（Christopher Elliott）介入聯繫美航後，航空公司再發192美元抵用金，總計442美元。美航承認機場人員曾提出補償方案，但拒付650美元，認為該金額可能是提供給自願讓位旅客的方案；艾略特的報導並未證實該名地勤人員是否有權保證較高金額。

聯邦法規14 CFR第250.6條規定，航空公司因營運或安全原因換用較小機型、且因此無法容納所有已確認訂位旅客時，旅客不適用非自願拒載賠償。符合資格的非自願拒載賠償依旅客抵達目的地的延誤而定，美國運輸部上限為單程票價200%、最高1075美元，延誤較長者為400%、最高2150美元；換用小機型的例外情形觸發時，這些金額並不自動適用。美國運輸部要求航空公司向被非自願拒載的旅客提供書面權益說明。此案發生在美航指示機場員工自2026年9月30日起停止非自願拒載的數週後；運輸部數據顯示，美航與其區域合作夥伴2025年共拒載14758名旅客，約占全行業24596件非自願拒載的60%。

en.title: American Airlines declines to pay promised $650, citing smaller aircraft
en.summary: American Airlines declined to honor a gate agent's reported $650 promise to a passenger denied boarding on a New York-Cleveland flight, saying an aircraft downgrade exempted it from federal involuntary denied-boarding compensation. The passenger ultimately received $442 in flight credits. The case surfaced weeks after American told staff to stop involuntarily bumping passengers.
body: American Airlines has declined to honor a gate agent's reported promise of $650 to a passenger denied boarding on a flight bound for Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE), saying an aircraft downgrade exempted it from federal involuntary denied-boarding compensation. Nicholle Acciarri was scheduled to fly from New York to Cleveland when she was denied boarding. She claimed that a gate agent offered a $650 check or reimbursement for a rental car, airline ticket, or hotel. Acciarri rented a car and drove to Cleveland, expecting American to cover the expense.

The airline initially provided a $250 flight credit that expired after one year. Customer relations later said she was not entitled to regulated compensation because the aircraft had been changed to a smaller model. One supervisor reportedly found records indicating eligibility for a $353 check or a $442 credit due to weight restrictions, but American subsequently described that entry as an error. After consumer advocate Christopher Elliott contacted the airline, American issued an additional $192 credit, bringing the total to $442. The carrier acknowledged that an agent had made an offer at the airport but declined to pay $650, suggesting that amount was likely intended for passengers volunteering to give up their seats. Elliott's report does not establish whether the gate agent had authority to guarantee the larger payment, leaving the dispute centred on the difference between the airport offer and the airline's later explanation.

Federal rules distinguish between passengers removed from oversold flights and those who cannot be accommodated after an airline substitutes a smaller aircraft for operational or safety reasons. Under 14 CFR 250.6, passengers are not eligible for involuntary denied-boarding compensation when a lower-capacity aircraft is substituted for those reasons and the change prevents the flight from accommodating everyone with confirmed reservations. For eligible involuntary bumps, compensation depends on the delay before passengers reach their destination on alternate transportation. Current Department of Transportation limits reach 200% of the one-way fare, capped at $1,075, for qualifying delays, and 400%, capped at $2,150, for longer delays. Those amounts do not apply automatically when the smaller-aircraft exception is triggered. The DOT requires airlines to provide involuntarily bumped passengers with a written explanation of their rights. The dispute surfaced weeks after American directed airport employees to stop involuntarily denying boarding, effective September 30, 2026. Department of Transportation figures cited by View From The Wing show American and its regional partners bumped 14,758 passengers in 2025, about 60% of the 24,596 involuntary denied boardings reported across the industry. American recorded more such cases than all other reporting airlines combined, although Frontier had the highest rate relative to passenger volume.
